propositions.text: The appellants Vidéotron and Groupe TVA appeal the Federal Court summary trial judgment by Justice Grammond on February 24, 2022.
propositions.quote: The appellants, Vidéotron Ltée (Vidéotron) and Groupe TVA inc. (Groupe TVA), are appealing from the judgment by way of summary trial rendered by Justice Grammond of the Federal Court (the Judge) on February 24, 2022 (2022 FC 256).

propositions.text: The Judge held Konek and Hill Valley jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in retransmitting Groupe TVA stations.
propositions.quote: the Judge held that the respondent companies, Technologies Konek inc. (Konek) and Coopérative de câblodistribution Hill Valley (Hill Valley), are jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in the retransmission of Groupe TVA stations

propositions.text: The Judge exonerated Libéo from liability for the infringements at issue.
propositions.quote: the Judge exonerated the respondent company Libéo inc. (Libéo) from any liability relating to the infringements at issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellants Vidéotron and Groupe TVA appeal the Federal Court judgment holding Konek and Hill Valley liable but exonerating Libéo.

propositions.text: Appellants ask the Court to find Libéo jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements due to direct involvement.
propositions.quote: the appellants are asking this Court to find Libéo jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for infringements of Groupe TVA’s copyright under the Copyright Act, R.S.C. (1985), c. C-42 (CA) because of its direct involvement in these infringements.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue Libéo should be held jointly liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements due to direct involvement.

propositions.text: The Court would allow the appeal after reviewing the record and arguments.
propositions.quote: Having carefully read the record and examined the oral and written arguments of the parties, I would allow the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it would allow the appeal after reviewing the record and arguments.

propositions.text: The Judge summarized the facts at paragraphs 8–17, which are reproduced as relevant for this appeal.
propositions.quote: The Judge aptly summarized the facts of this case (Judge’s decision at paras. 8–17). It is therefore appropriate to reproduce the most relevant of these facts for the purposes of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Judge summarized the facts at paragraphs 8–17 and reproduces relevant facts for this appeal.

propositions.text: TVA Group is a Canadian broadcaster owning TVA and TVA Sports stations.
propositions.quote: The appellant TVA Group is a Canadian television broadcaster that owns and operates a number of television stations, including TVA and TVA Sports.

propositions.text: Vidéotron is a broadcasting distribution undertaking (BDU) that retransmits TVA and TVA Sports stations to subscribers.
propositions.quote: The appellant Vidéotron is a broadcasting distribution undertaking (BDU) under the Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11. As a BDU, Vidéotron receives and retransmits a number of television stations to its subscribers, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states TVA Group owns TVA stations and Vidéotron is a BDU retransmitting these stations to subscribers.

propositions.text: Libéo, founded in 1996, operates in IT and website hosting; Rousseau was CEO until 2019, Bussière president since 2016.
propositions.quote: The respondent Libéo, founded in 1996 (under the name Technologies Sys-Tech) by Jean-François Rousseau, is a company that operates in the information technology and website‑hosting field. Jean-François Rousseau was Libéo’s chief executive officer until 2019, and Joé Bussière has been its president since 2016.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Libéo is an IT and hosting company founded in 1996; Rousseau was CEO until 2019, Bussière president since 2016.

propositions.text: In 2016, Rousseau partnered with Michaud to form Konek Technologies Inc. to design hotel technological solutions.
propositions.quote: In 2016, while he was Libéo’s chief executive officer, Jean-François Rousseau began a partnership with Louis Michaud to design new technological solutions for hotels. To that end, they formed Konek Technologies Inc.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Rousseau and Michaud formed Konek Technologies Inc. in 2016 to design hotel technological solutions.

propositions.text: In 2018, Konek designed the 'Konek box' under contract with Libéo, enabling hotel TVs to retransmit stations.
propositions.quote: A few years later, under a contract with Libéo in 2018, Konek designed a product known as the [translation] “Konek box”. This box allows televisions in hotel rooms to perform several functions, including retransmitting a number of television stations in hotel rooms.

propositions.text: Rousseau gradually disengaged from Libéo and left CEO position in 2019.
propositions.quote: In the years following the contract between Konek and Libéo, Jean-François Rousseau gradually disengaged from his responsibilities at Libéo and left his position as chief executive officer in 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Konek designed the 'Konek box' for Libéo in 2018; Rousseau left Libéo CEO role in 2019.

propositions.text: In February 2020, Rousseau helped form Hill Valley to provide more TV stations to hotels subscribing to Konek’s services.
propositions.quote: In February 2020, Jean-François Rousseau was involved in forming Hill Valley with the aim of providing a broader range of television stations to hotels subscribing to Konek’s services.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Rousseau helped form Hill Valley in 2020 to provide more TV stations to hotels subscribing to Konek.

propositions.text: Hill Valley applied to CRTC for BDU exemption on December 30, 2020; approved February 3, 2021.
propositions.quote: On December 30, 2020, Hill Valley applied to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to be recognized as a BDU exempt from the requirements of the Broadcasting Act while being subject to a more limited set of obligations. The CRTC approved Hill Valley’s application for exemption on February 3, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Hill Valley applied for and received CRTC BDU exemption between December 2020 and February 2021.

propositions.text: Vidéotron discovered Konek and Hill Valley retransmitted TVA stations via Internet in hotel rooms in 2020.
propositions.quote: Having become aware of Konek’s television station retransmission activities in 2020, Vidéotron ran various checks in hotel rooms served by Konek. The results of the checks performed by Vidéotron showed that Konek and Hill Valley were using the Internet to retransmit content, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations, to their subscribers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Vidéotron found Konek and Hill Valley retransmitting TVA stations via Internet in hotels in 2020.

propositions.text: On February 26, 2021, appellants sued Konek, Hill Valley, Libéo and their directors for copyright infringement and terminated Libéo's service contract.
propositions.quote: Therefore, on February 26, 2021, the appellants instituted proceedings in the Federal Court, alleging that Konek, Hill Valley and Libéo as well as their directing minds (Jean-François Rousseau, Joé Bussière and Louis Michaud) infringed TVA Group’s copyright by communicating to the public by telecommunication programs broadcast on the TVA and TVA Sports stations without authorization or without having previously obtained a licence for this purpose. On the same day, Vidéotron sent Libéo a notice of termination of the service contract between them for the decoders used to retransmit the feed from the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellants sued Konek, Hill Valley, Libéo and directors for copyright infringement and terminated Libéo's contract on February 26, 2021.

propositions.text: The Judge set out summary trial framework and agreed to limit trial to corporate entities, excluding directors' liability.
propositions.quote: Before addressing the merits of the case, the Judge set out the framework for a summary trial and then agreed with the parties that it was appropriate in the circumstances to proceed by way of summary trial pursuant to rule 216 of the Federal Courts Rules, SOR/98-106 (Tremblay v. Orio Canada Inc., 2013 FC 109, [2014] 3 F.C.R. 404 at para. 24). Before the Judge, the parties agreed that the issue of directors’ liability should not be decided at the summary trial and that the debate should therefore be limited to the corporate entities, namely, Konek, Libéo and Hill Valley.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge set summary trial framework and limited issues to corporate entities, excluding directors' liability.

propositions.text: Appellants argued Konek, Libéo and Hill Valley infringed copyright by retransmitting TVA stations.
propositions.quote: The appellants (plaintiffs) therefore argued that the respondents Konek, Libéo and Hill Valley (defendants) had infringed their copyright by retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

propositions.text: Respondents argued retransmission was exempt under section 31 of the Copyright Act, so no infringement occurred.
propositions.quote: For their part, the respondents (defendants) replied that the said retransmission was covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA and that the appellants’ (plaintiffs’) copyright had therefore not been infringed.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge reports appellants argued infringement by retransmission; respondents claimed exemption under section 31 of the Copyright Act.

propositions.text: The Judge found retransmission of TVA Sports not covered by section 31 exemption.
propositions.quote: The retransmission of TVA Sports is not covered by section 31 of the CA (Judge’s decision at paras. 45, 100).

propositions.text: Before February 3, 2021, Konek and Hill Valley did not qualify as retransmitters under section 31 and could not claim exemption for TVA retransmission.
propositions.quote: Prior to February 3, 2021, neither Konek nor Hill Valley qualified as a “retransmitter” under section 31 of the CA. Therefore, they could not avail themselves of the exemption set out in the CA for the retransmission of TVA (Judge’s decision at paras. 53–54, 100).

propositions.text: Konek and Hill Valley are jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in retransmitting TVA and TVA Sports stations not covered by exemption.
propositions.quote: Konek and Hill Valley are jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements committed by either corporation in the retransmission of the TVA and TVA Sports stations, where such retransmission is not covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA (Judge’s decision at paras. 95, 101).

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found TVA Sports retransmission not exempt, Konek and Hill Valley not retransmitters before Feb 3, 2021, and liable for infringements.

propositions.text: Judge found Konek and Hill Valley liable for copyright infringement but exonerated Libéo from liability.
propositions.quote: The Judge thus determined that two of the three corporate entities concerned, namely, Konek and Hill Valley, were jointly and severally liable for infringing the appellant TVA Group’s copyright when the retransmissions were not covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA. However, he expressed the view that Libéo, the third corporate entity concerned, was not liable for the copyright infringements committed by Konek and Hill Valley in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations (Declaratory Judgment at paras. 4–5).

propositions.text: Appellants challenge the Judge’s finding exonerating Libéo from copyright infringement liability.
propositions.quote: In this appeal, the appellants are challenging the Judge’s finding exonerating Libéo from copyright infringements in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found Konek and Hill Valley liable but exonerated Libéo; appellants challenge Libéo's exoneration.

propositions.text: Court allowed Mr. Spicer to make brief representations on subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) of the Copyright Act, but these are not at issue here.
propositions.quote: It should be noted that, during the hearing, this Court exceptionally allowed Mr. Spicer to make brief representations on behalf of the respondents relating to subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) of the CA, even though Mr. Spicer did not appear on the record. Be that as it may, these subsections are not at issue in this appeal, and there is therefore no need to rule on their scope.

paragraphs.summary: The court allowed Mr. Spicer to make brief representations on certain subsections, but these are not at issue in this appeal.

propositions.text: Standard of review is correctness for questions of law, palpable and overriding error for fact or mixed fact and law (Housen v. Nikolaisen).
propositions.quote: The applicable standard of review in this case is set out in Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235 (Housen). The standard of correctness applies to questions of law (Housen at para. 8), but findings of fact or questions of mixed fact and law are reviewable only where the trial judge has made a palpable and overriding error (Housen at paras. 10, 36).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is correctness for law and palpable error for fact or mixed questions, per Housen v. Nikolaisen.

propositions.text: Issue is whether the Judge erred in applying the legal principles and correctly identified the legal framework.
propositions.quote: This appeal raises the issue of whether the Judge erred in his application of the applicable legal principles. More specifically, did the Judge correctly identify the legal framework on which his analysis is based?

propositions.text: If trial judge uses wrong legal principle, no deference is owed (Canada (Commissioner of Official Languages) v. Canada (Employment and Social Development)).
propositions.quote: as this Court recently mentioned in Canada (Commissioner of Official Languages) v. Canada (Employment and Social Development), 2022 FCA 14, [2022] F.C.J. No. 72 (QL) at paragraph 109, “[i]f the trial judge conducts his analysis on the basis of the wrong legal principle, no deference is owed.”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether the Judge erred in legal framework application; no deference if wrong legal principle used.

propositions.text: It is undisputed that Groupe TVA owns copyright in many programs broadcast on TVA and TVA Sports stations.
propositions.quote: Although the Judge remained silent on the issue of ownership of rights, it is not disputed in this case that Groupe TVA owns the copyright in Canada to a wide variety of programs. Some of these programs are produced directly or through its subsidiary and are then broadcast on a number of television stations, including TVA and TVA Sports.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it is undisputed that Groupe TVA owns copyright in many programs broadcast on TVA and TVA Sports stations.

propositions.text: Under subsection 3(1) of the CA, Groupe TVA has the sole right to communicate its programs to the public by telecommunication.
propositions.quote: Thus, under subsection 3(1) of the CA, Groupe TVA has, among other things, the sole right to communicate Groupe TVA Programs to the public by telecommunication: Copyright and Moral Rights in Works Droit d’auteur et droits moraux sur les œuvres Copyright Droit d’auteur Copyright in works Droit d’auteur sur l’œuvre 3 (1) For the purposes of this Act, copyright, in relation to a work, means the sole right to produce or reproduce the work or any substantial part thereof in any material form whatever, to perform the work or any substantial part thereof in public or, if the work is unpublished, to publish the work or any substantial part thereof, and includes the sole right 3 (1) Le droit d’auteur sur l’œuvre comporte le droit exclusif de produire ou reproduire la totalité ou une partie importante de l’œuvre, sous une forme matérielle quelconque, d’en exécuter ou d’en représenter la totalité ou une partie importante en public et, si l’œuvre n’est pas publiée, d’en publier la totalité ou une partie importante; ce droit comporte, en outre, le droit exclusif : … […] (f) in the case of any literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, to communicate the work to the public by telecommunication, f) de communiquer au public, par télécommunication, une œuvre littéraire, dramatique, musicale ou artistique; … […] and to authorize any such acts. Est inclus dans la présente définition le droit exclusif d’autoriser ces actes.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that under subsection 3(1) of the CA, Groupe TVA has the sole right to communicate its programs to the public by telecommunication.

propositions.text: In CCH, the Supreme Court held that subsection 3(1) includes the right to authorize acts and authorization can be inferred from acts or indifference.
propositions.quote: In CCH Canadian Ltd. v. Law Society of Upper Canada, 2004 SCC 13, [2004] 1 S.C.R. 339 (CCH), the Supreme Court of Canada stated that subsection 3(1) of the CA includes the right to authorize any of the acts set out in that subsection. The Supreme Court also discussed the issues involved in determining whether copyright infringement was authorized. It ruled that to authorize means to “[g]ive approval to; sanction, permit; favour, encourage” and that it can be inferred from acts or indifference: Authorization is a question of fact that depends on the circumstances of each particular case and can be inferred from acts that are less than direct and positive, including a sufficient degree of indifference. However, a person does not authorize infringement by authorizing the mere use of equipment that could be used to infringe copyright. Courts should presume that a person who authorizes an activity does so only so far as it is in accordance with the law. [Citations omitted.] (CCH at para. 38)

paragraphs.summary: The Supreme Court in CCH held subsection 3(1) includes the right to authorize acts, which can be inferred from acts or indifference.

propositions.text: The presumption of authorization may be rebutted by showing a relationship or control between the authorizer and infringers.
propositions.quote: In CCH, the Supreme Court was careful to point out in the same paragraph that the presumption of authorization may also be rebutted on the basis of the relationship that exists between the alleged authorizer and the persons who committed the copyright infringement: This presumption may be rebutted if it is shown that a certain relationship or degree of control existed between the alleged authorizer and the persons who committed the copyright infringement. [Citations omitted.] (CCH at para. 38)

paragraphs.summary: The Supreme Court in CCH said the presumption of authorization can be rebutted by showing a relationship or control between authorizer and infringers.

propositions.text: This Court in Sirius Canada said CCH does not require a legal relationship to rebut the presumption of authorization; other circumstances suffice.
propositions.quote: In Sirius Canada Inc. v. CMRRA/SODRAC Inc., 2010 FCA 348, [2012] 3 F.C.R. 717, this Court expressed the view that CCH did not “necessarily [require] a particular legal relationship between the user of equipment and the person authorizing its use” to rebut the presumption (at para. 26). In other words, the presumption can be rebutted in other circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: This Court said CCH does not require a legal relationship to rebut authorization presumption; other circumstances suffice.

propositions.text: Paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA excludes from the Act a person who only provides telecommunication means for another to communicate a work.
propositions.quote: Paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA provides that certain activities are excluded from the application of the CA. The provision reads as follows: Communication to the public by telecommunication Communication au public par télécommunication 2.4 (1) For the purposes of communication to the public by telecommunication, 2.4 (1) Les règles qui suivent s’appliquent dans les cas de communication au public par télécommunication : … […] (b) a person whose only act in respect of the communication of a work or other subject-matter to the public consists of providing the means of telecommunication necessary for another person to so communicate the work or other subject-matter does not communicate that work or other subject-matter to the public; and b) n’effectue pas une communication au public la personne qui ne fait que fournir à un tiers les moyens de télécommunication nécessaires pour que celui-ci l’effectue; … […]

paragraphs.summary: The court states paragraph 2.4(1)(b) excludes from the Act a person who only provides telecommunication means for another to communicate a work.

propositions.text: SOCAN and Lackman cases hold that an intermediary acting as a conduit without knowledge or influence is protected under paragraph 2.4(1)(b).
propositions.quote: This paragraph was interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada in Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada v. Canadian Assn. of Internet Providers, 2004 SCC 45, [2004] 2 S.C.R. 427 (SOCAN), and recently by this Court in Bell Canada v. Lackman, 2018 FCA 42, [2018] F.C.R. 199 (Lackman). The principle that flows from paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA can be summarized as follows: an intermediary who is in fact merely acting as a “channel of communication”, has no knowledge of the content and allows others to communicate without influencing the content, will be considered a “conduit” and, as such, will benefit from the protection conferred by paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA and will not unjustly fall under the definition in paragraph 3(1)(f) mentioned above (SOCAN at paras. 90, 92, 101; Lackman at paras. 4, 27–33).

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN and Lackman hold an intermediary acting as a conduit without knowledge or influence is protected under paragraph 2.4(1)(b).

propositions.text: Paragraph 31.1(1) of the CA exempts persons providing Internet or digital network services from copyright infringement solely for providing telecommunication means.
propositions.quote: Finally, paragraph 31.1(1) of the CA contains another exemption that may be cited regarding certain activities of Internet retransmitters to avoid the application of the CA: Network services Services réseau Network services Services réseau 31.1 (1) A person who, in providing services related to the operation of the Internet or another digital network, provides any means for the telecommunication or the reproduction of a work or other subject-matter through the Internet or that other network does not, solely by reason of providing those means, infringe copyright in that work or other subject-matter. 31.1 (1) La personne qui, dans le cadre de la prestation de services liés à l’exploitation d’Internet ou d’un autre réseau numérique, fournit des moyens permettant la télécommunication ou la reproduction d’une œuvre ou de tout autre objet du droit d’auteur par l’intermédiaire d’Internet ou d’un autre réseau ne viole pas le droit d’auteur sur l’œuvre ou l’autre objet du seul fait qu’elle fournit ces moyens.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 31.1(1) exempts persons providing Internet or digital network services from copyright infringement solely for providing telecommunication means.

propositions.text: The Judge erred in requiring proof of fraud, abuse of right or public order contravention to lift Libéo's corporate veil.
propositions.quote: The appellants submit that the Judge erred in finding that Libéo was not liable for the infringement committed by Konek and Hill Valley on the grounds that the appellants did not establish the “fraud, abuse of right or contravention of a rule of public order” (art. 317 of the Civil Code of Québec (CCQ)) required to lift the corporate veil between Konek, Hill Valley and Libéo.

propositions.text: Lifting the corporate veil was not an issue the Judge had to decide, so proof was not required.
propositions.quote: The appellants allege that they did not have to establish this, as requested by the Judge, because lifting the corporate veil and disregarding Libéo’s distinct legal personality was not one of the issues that the Judge had to decide.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the Judge erred by requiring proof of fraud or abuse to lift Libéo's corporate veil, which was not an issue before him.

propositions.text: The Judge did not err given the evidence at summary trial; no palpable and overriding error occurred.
propositions.quote: For its part, the respondent Libéo essentially argues that, given the evidence submitted to the Judge at the summary trial, he did not commit a palpable and overriding error that would warrant intervention by this Court.

propositions.text: The Judge ruled on issues not submitted, including when Hill Valley qualified as a BDU, which was unnecessary as no cross-appeal was filed.
propositions.quote: However, like the appellants, the respondents also criticize the Judge for ruling on issues that were not submitted to him by the parties. More specifically, they argue that the issues submitted to the Judge did not include determining when Hill Valley qualified as a BDU. According to the respondents, the Judge therefore did not have to rule on the periods that had not been specified and submitted by the parties at the summary trial (Respondents’ Memorandum of Fact and Law at paras. 29–32). However, since no cross-appeal was filed, the issue is not before us, and there is therefore no need for this Court to address it.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Judge did not err given the evidence and that ruling on unsubmitted issues is not before this Court.

propositions.text: The issue of lifting Libéo’s corporate veil was not submitted to the Judge and proof was not required.
propositions.quote: At the hearing before this Court, the appellants insisted that the issue of lifting Libéo’s corporate veil had not been submitted to the Judge. They allege that they did not have to establish this, as requested by the Judge, because lifting the corporate veil and disregarding Libéo’s distinct legal personality was not one of the issues that the Judge had to decide.

propositions.text: Libéo concedes appellants did not refer to the corporate veil but Judge applied the principle because appellants argued companies were inseparable.
propositions.quote: For its part, Libéo concedes that the appellants did not refer to the corporate veil but asserts that the Judge applied the principle because the appellants argued that the companies were intrinsically linked or inseparable.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants say corporate veil issue was not submitted; Libéo concedes but says Judge applied it due to appellants' inseparability argument.

propositions.text: The plaintiffs contended Konek and Hill Valley are one and the same and Libéo is liable for leasing decoders used to retransmit TVA programs.
propositions.quote: The plaintiffs essentially contend that Konek and Hill Valley are one and the same. They also claim that Libéo is liable because it leased from Vidéotron decoders that, until March 1, 2021, were used to retransmit TVA and TVA Sports. Libéo therefore actively participated in infringing Groupe TVA’s copyright.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found plaintiffs contended Konek and Hill Valley are the same and Libéo liable for leasing decoders used to retransmit TVA.

propositions.text: The Judge examined lifting the corporate veil and found no fraud or abuse to override separate legal personalities, so Libéo not liable.
propositions.quote: The fact that the same people are shareholders or directors of Konek and Libéo does not override the separate legal personalities of these corporations. The shareholders or directors of a corporation may create different corporations to operate different businesses. As I explained above, it is only in cases of fraud, abuse of right or contravention of a rule of public order that the corporate veil is lifted. The plaintiffs proved no such thing. The close ties between the two corporations or the fact that on its website, Libéo stated that it founded Konek do not mean that the two corporations’ distinct legal personalities can be ignored.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found no fraud or abuse to lift the corporate veil and thus Libéo not liable for Konek and Hill Valley's infringements.

propositions.text: Appellants did not allege Libéo liable through lifting the corporate veil but for direct fault of communicating programs by telecommunication.
propositions.quote: In fact, the appellants did not allege at trial that Libéo should be held liable for Konek and Hill Valley’s faults (fault of another) through the lifting of the corporate veil. Rather, the appellants alleged that Libéo was liable for copyright infringements for having directly communicated Groupe TVA’s programs by telecommunication (direct fault).

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Libéo's liability was for direct fault, not via lifting the corporate veil.

propositions.text: Judge applied incorrect legal framework by focusing on lifting corporate veil and fault of another, not Libéo's direct fault.
propositions.quote: In adopting the legal framework of the lifting of the corporate veil on grounds of “fraud, abuse of right or contravention of a rule of public order” (art. 317 of the CCQ), the Judge’s analysis necessarily focused on the issue of Libéo’s liability through the lens of the fault of another, namely, that of Konek and Hill Valley, while it was Libéo’s direct fault that was at issue. By introducing the lifting of the corporate veil with regard to Libéo’s liability, the Judge therefore applied an incorrect legal framework, which led him to err in his analysis of the evidence because, among other things, he was seeking evidence of “fraud or abuse of right” to lift the corporate veil, while Libéo’s direct fault was the sole issue. It is important to note that, if the Judge was concerned about the corporate veil issue, he had to ask the parties to make submissions on this matter and, if necessary, additional representations. Since he did not do so, he was required to decide all the issues on the basis of the record and the arguments submitted to him. This was his role (CXS Transportation, Inc. v. ABB Inc., 2022 FCA 96).

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Judge erred by applying lifting corporate veil framework instead of focusing on Libéo's direct fault.

propositions.text: Had Judge applied correct legal framework, he would have found Libéo liable for copyright infringement.
propositions.quote: Thus, had the Judge based his analysis on the appropriate legal framework, I am of the view that, in light of the evidence presented, he would have had to find Libéo liable for infringing Groupe TVA’s copyright.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants conclude Judge would have found Libéo liable if correct legal framework applied.

propositions.text: Judge relied on Rousseau's and Bussière's testimony to find Libéo not liable for copyright infringements by Konek and Hill Valley.
propositions.quote: The plaintiffs rely on a particular fact to hold Libéo liable. Until March 1, 2021, Konek or Hill Valley, as the case may be, picked up TVA and TVA Sports using Illico decoders leased from Vidéotron. These decoders were in Libéo’s server room and they were registered to Libéo by Vidéotron. I find this to be a very thin basis for holding Libéo liable. First, Mr. Rousseau testified that he himself ordered these decoders from Vidéotron and that the fees were always paid for by Konek. He also supervised the installation of these decoders in Libéo’s server room. Mr. Bussière, on the other hand, states that he had not been aware of the presence of these decoders or their use. Second, even if the lease agreement for these decoders is deemed to have been between Vidéotron and Libéo, there is no evidence that Libéo was aware of the specific use of these decoders by Konek and Hill Valley. Ultimately, the plaintiffs rely on the fact that the same individual, Mr. Rousseau, was in fact the head of both Konek and Libéo. However, this is not a sufficient basis to treat the two corporations as one. Libéo is therefore not liable for any copyright infringements committed by Konek or Hill Valley.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found Libéo not liable relying on Rousseau's and Bussière's testimony about decoders and lack of awareness.

propositions.text: All evidence contradicts the Judge’s finding that Libéo is not liable.
propositions.quote: With respect, all the evidence in the record, analyzed within the correct legal framework, contradicts the Judge’s finding.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue all evidence contradicts Judge's finding that Libéo is not liable.

propositions.text: Rousseau and Bussière have overlapping roles in Libéo and Konek; Rousseau founded Libéo and remains majority shareholder with ultimate control.
propositions.quote: It should be noted that Jean-François Rousseau and Joé Bussière have a long-standing business relationship and collaborate in various information technology companies. More specifically, they hold important overlapping roles within Libéo and Konek. Jean-François Rousseau founded Libéo in 1996 (under the name Technologies Sys-Tech). Libéo’s main goal is developing technological solutions and infrastructure and hosting servers and websites (Judge’s decision at para. 9). Its head office is located at 300‑5700 Des Galeries Boulevard in Québec. Jean-François Rousseau was its president until 2016 and its chief executive officer until March 2019. In fact, he then stayed with the company for several months, even though he had officially left to work for Konek (Appeal Book, tab 24 at 150–53). He was also its secretary‑treasurer, director and majority shareholder. He still remains Libéo’s majority shareholder with [translation] “ultimate control” (Appeal Book, tab 24 at 20–22). Joé Bussière replaced Jean-François Rousseau as president of Libéo in 2016 and remains its second largest shareholder. It appears that Libéo is a small business composed of two directors: Jean-François Rousseau and Joé Bussière.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Rousseau and Bussière have overlapping roles in Libéo and Konek; Rousseau founded Libéo and remains majority shareholder.

propositions.text: Konek was co-founded by Rousseau and Bussière; it provides TV and internet services for hotels and shared premises with Libéo until 2019.
propositions.quote: Konek was co-founded by Joé Bussière and Jean-François Rousseau. Mr. Bussière is a director and equal shareholder with Jean-François Rousseau. Konek provides integrated TV, IP telephony, Internet and Wi-Fi services for hotels. “Konek boxes” installed in hotel rooms provide access to a large number of live television stations, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations (Judge’s decision at paras. 10, 98). Since its founding until September 2019, Konek shared the same premises as Libéo at the same address (300-5700 Des Galeries Boulevard in Québec). Since September 2019, Konek has been located next to Libéo at 302-5700 Des Galeries Boulevard in Québec.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Konek was co-founded by Rousseau and Bussière; it provides TV and internet services and shared premises with Libéo until 2019.

propositions.text: Libéo played an important role in Konek after 2018 contract, knowing Konek would use its infrastructure for TV services.
propositions.quote: After entering into a contract with Konek in 2018, Libéo played an important role in Konek. When it signed the contract, Libéo knew that Konek was going to provide its television services using its infrastructure, including encoding capture servers (Appeal Book, tab 26 at 59–61, 64–66).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Libéo played an important role in Konek after 2018 contract, knowing Konek would use its infrastructure for TV services.

propositions.text: Libéo was involved in developing Konek's infrastructure after signing the contract.
propositions.quote: after signing the contract, Libéo was involved in developing several aspects of Konek’s infrastructure

propositions.text: Libéo designed and supplied 'Konek boxes'.
propositions.quote: designing and supplying “Konek boxes” (Judge’s decision at para. 10)

propositions.text: Libéo developed software for the Konek boxes.
propositions.quote: developing software for the boxes (Judge’s decision at para. 96)

propositions.text: Libéo provided infrastructure and servers needed to operate Konek services, including encoding capture servers.
propositions.quote: providing the infrastructure and servers needed to operate Konek services, including “encoding capture servers” for television content (Judge’s decision at paras. 96, 99 and Appeal Book, tab 26 at 64–66)

paragraphs.summary: The court states Libéo developed Konek's infrastructure, designed and supplied Konek boxes, developed software, and provided servers.

propositions.text: In August 2019, Libéo subscribed to Vidéotron television services.
propositions.quote: In August 2019, Libéo subscribed to Vidéotron television services.

propositions.text: Joé Bussière confirmed a Vidéotron technician accessed Libéo's secure room during ILLICO decoder installation.
propositions.quote: Joé Bussière confirmed that, when the ILLICO decoders were being installed, a Vidéotron technician had access to Libéo’s secure room

propositions.text: A Libéo director knew the server room contained ILLICO terminals.
propositions.quote: a Libéo director knew that the server room contained ILLICO terminals

propositions.text: Jean-François Rousseau personally gave Vidéotron technician access to Libéo server room and still had access as of Sept 27, 2021.
propositions.quote: Jean-François Rousseau confirmed that he had personally given the Vidéotron technician access to the Libéo server room because he himself had access to it... as of the date of his cross-examination, September 27, 2021, he still had access to Libéo’s server room.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts evidence that Libéo subscribed to Vidéotron, and technicians had access to Libéo's server room with ILLICO terminals.

propositions.text: Some ILLICO decoders hosted by Libéo were tuned to TVA Sports and retransmitted to hotels.
propositions.quote: some of the ILLICO decoders hosted by Libéo were constantly tuned to TVA Group’s TVA Sports station and then retransmitted to hotels

propositions.text: Respondents claim Konek paid for ILLICO decoders, so Libéo did not retransmit TVA content and is not liable.
propositions.quote: it was Konek who paid for them directly, and Libéo “is therefore not the one who retransmitted the TVA and TVA Sports content” and, consequently, was not liable

propositions.text: The court rejects respondents' argument and finds Libéo responsible for use of rented ILLICO decoders on its premises.
propositions.quote: This argument is without merit... Libéo was responsible for the way it used these decoders, located on its premises.

paragraphs.summary: The respondents argue Libéo is not liable for retransmission, but the court rejects this and finds Libéo responsible for decoder use.

propositions.text: A document from Libéo's website describes a partnership and alliance with Konek, highlighting Libéo's innovation role.
propositions.quote: describes the relationship between Libéo and Konek as one of “partnership” and “alliance” and indicates that “Libéo’s innovation skills are at the heart of Konek.ai’s success”

paragraphs.summary: The court notes a Libéo website document showing a partnership and alliance with Konek, emphasizing Libéo's innovation.

propositions.text: It is difficult to find Libéo unaware of the use of decoders; evidence shows Libéo subscribed and retransmitted TVA content illegally.
propositions.quote: it is extremely difficult to find that “there is no evidence that Libéo was aware of the specific use”... Libéo has subscribed to Vidéotron’s television services... and retransmits it illegally

propositions.text: Libéo directly participated and cannot claim exemptions under the CA.
propositions.quote: I am of the view that the evidence has established Libéo’s direct participation, and Libéo is therefore not in a position to avail itself of the exemptions set out in the CA.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Libéo directly participated in illegal retransmission and cannot claim exemptions under the CA.

propositions.text: Appellants submit the Judge erred by not ordering a permanent injunction against Konek and Hill Valley after finding section 31 CA did not apply.
propositions.quote: the appellants submit that... the Judge should have ordered a permanent injunction against Konek and Hill Valley and that he erred in law

propositions.text: Appellants ask the Court to address the injunction issue in obiter due to limited case law on summary trials.
propositions.quote: The appellants are not asking this Court to decide this issue as a separate ground of appeal, but to address it in obiter because “there is little case law on the scope of summary trials

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the Judge erred by not ordering a permanent injunction and ask the Court to address this issue in obiter.

propositions.text: The Court declines to address the injunction issue abstractly as it was resubmitted to the Judge at trial.
propositions.quote: I do not find it appropriate for this Court to address this issue in the abstract... the injunction issue was resubmitted to the Judge at trial.

propositions.text: The Judge found Konek and Hill Valley jointly liable but declined to rule on injunction due to agreement on summary trial scope.
propositions.quote: the Judge held that Konek and Hill Valley were jointly and severally liable... but... declined to rule on the injunction... on the basis of the agreement between the parties

propositions.text: The appellants face further proceedings and costs despite infringement finding, which seems contrary to proportionality and sound justice administration.
propositions.quote: the appellants have paradoxically found themselves... despite a finding of copyright infringements... will have to institute further proceedings and incur further costs... appears to run counter to proportionality and the sound administration of justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court refuses to address the injunction issue now, noting appellants face further proceedings despite infringement finding, which seems unjust.

propositions.text: The Court allows the appeal, sets aside part of the judgment, and declares Libéo liable for copyright infringements jointly with Konek and Hill Valley.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal, set aside the judgment in part... to declare Libéo liable for the copyright infringements... and jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, sets aside part of the judgment, and declares Libéo jointly liable for copyright infringements.
